theory.intro: Summary statistics from grouped data are **estimates** because the **class centre** represents every score in that class.
facts: The **estimated mean** of grouped data is $\overline{x} = \dfrac{\Sigma (cc \times f)}{\Sigma f}$, where $cc$ is the class centre and $f$ is frequency.
The **modal class** is the class interval with the highest frequency, reported as an interval rather than a single frequency.

For an odd number of scores, the **median class** contains the score at position $\dfrac{n+1}{2}$. For an even number, check positions $\dfrac{n}{2}$ and $\dfrac{n}{2}+1$: if both lie in the same class, that is the median class; if they lie in different classes, the grouped table may not determine a unique class for their average.
To **estimate the median from an ogive**, read horizontally from $50\%$ of total cumulative frequency to the curve, then down to the axis.
Grouped statistics are **approximations** because using the class centre may give a different mean from the exact mean; the grouped estimate can also equal the exact mean.
An **open-ended class** (such as '$> 60$' or '$70+$') has no class centre, preventing calculation of the estimated mean.
steps: Find the class centre ($cc$) for each class interval.
Multiply each class centre by its frequency to form the $cc \times f$ column.
Sum the frequencies ($\Sigma f$) and the products ($\Sigma cc \times f$).
Calculate the estimated mean: $\overline{x} = \dfrac{\Sigma (cc \times f)}{\Sigma f}$.

Identify the modal class (highest frequency). Use cumulative frequencies to locate the middle observation for odd $n$, or both middle observations for even $n$; if the two middle observations lie in different classes, their average may not have a uniquely determined class. For an ogive estimate, read across from $50\%$ of the total cumulative frequency, then down to the axis.

workedExamples.question_text:
The table shows the masses of parcels.

| Mass $m$ (kg) | Frequency $f$ |
|---|---:|
| $0<m\le2$ | 4 |
| $2<m\le6$ | 8 |
| $6<m\le12$ | 6 |
| $12<m\le20$ | 2 |

Estimate the mean mass, correct to 2 decimal places.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Each class centre is the average of its two endpoints. For the first class, $cc=\dfrac{0+2}{2}=1$.

| Mass $m$ (kg) | $f$ | $cc$ | $cc\times f$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| $0<m\le2$ | 4 | 1 | 4 |
| $2<m\le6$ | 8 | 4 | 32 |
| $6<m\le12$ | 6 | 9 | 54 |
| $12<m\le20$ | 2 | 16 | 32 |
| Total | 20 | | 122 |

$\begin{align*}\overline{x}&=\frac{\Sigma(cc\times f)}{\Sigma f}\\&=\frac{122}{20}\\&=6.10\text{ kg}\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text:
The table shows the ages of visitors to a museum.

| Age $a$ (years) | Frequency |
|---|---:|
| $0<a\le20$ | 6 |
| $20<a\le40$ | 10 |
| $40<a\le60$ | 9 |
| $60<a\le80$ | 6 |

(a) State the modal class and find the median class.

(b) One more visitor, aged 70, joins the group. Find the median class for the resulting 32 visitors.

(c) A separate group has frequencies 6, 10, 10 and 6 in the same four classes. Explain whether its median class can be determined uniquely.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) The highest frequency is 10, so the modal class is $20<a\le40$.

$\begin{align*}n&=6+10+9+6\\&=31\\\text{Median position}&=\frac{31+1}{2}\\&=16\end{align*}$

The cumulative frequencies are 6, 16, 25 and 31. The 16th visitor lies in $20<a\le40$, so this is the median class.

(b) The cumulative frequencies become 6, 16, 25 and 32. The middle observations are at positions 16 and 17. They lie in $20<a\le40$ and $40<a\le60$, respectively. Their exact ages are unknown, so their average could lie in either class. A unique median class cannot be determined.

(c) The cumulative frequencies are 6, 16, 26 and 32. Again, positions 16 and 17 lie in different classes. A unique median class cannot be determined from the grouped table.

workedExamples.question_text:
Five travel times are $12,13,14,15,16$ minutes. They are grouped into the single class $10<t\le20$.

(a) Calculate the exact mean and the grouped mean estimate.

(b) Explain why the grouped mean is an estimate and why it is higher in this case.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) $\begin{align*}\text{Exact mean}&=\frac{12+13+14+15+16}{5}\\&=\frac{70}{5}\\&=14\text{ min}\end{align*}$

$\begin{align*}cc&=\frac{10+20}{2}\\&=15\\\text{Grouped mean estimate}&=\frac{15\times5}{5}\\&=15\text{ min}\end{align*}$

(b) Grouping loses the individual values. The calculation replaces each value with the class centre, 15 minutes. The actual mean is 14 minutes, so the estimate is 1 minute higher. A grouped estimate can be higher, lower or equal to the exact mean.

workedExamples.question_text:
The table shows the ages of concert attendees.

| Age $a$ (years) | Frequency |
|---|---:|
| $16<a\le30$ | 12 |
| $30<a\le45$ | 18 |
| $45<a\le65$ | 14 |
| $65<a$ | 6 |

Explain why the class-centre method cannot give an estimated mean age from this table.
workedExamples.solution_text: The class $65<a$ has no upper endpoint, so its class centre cannot be calculated. The class-centre method needs a centre for every class with a nonzero frequency.

foundation.question_text:
A grouped frequency table is shown below.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Class interval}&\text{Frequency }(f)\\ \hline 10-19&6\\ 20-29&15\\ 30-39&9\end{array}$
State the modal class.
foundation.solution_text:
The greatest frequency is $15$, which corresponds to the interval $20 - 29$.
$\text{Modal class} = 20 - 29$

foundation.question_text:
A dataset of $25$ items has the following grouped distribution:
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Class interval}&\text{Frequency }(f)\\ \hline 0-4&4\\ 5-9&9\\ 10-14&8\\ 15-19&4\end{array}$
Find the median position and determine the median class.
foundation.solution_text:
$\text{Position} = \frac{25 + 1}{2}$
$= 13$
$\text{Cumulative frequencies: } 4, 13, 21, 25$
The $13\text{th}$ score lies in the interval $5 - 9$.
$\text{Median class} = 5 - 9$

foundation.question_text:
A grouped frequency table has two classes: $0-9$ ($cc = 4.5, f = 4$) and $10-19$ ($cc = 14.5, f = 6$).
Calculate $\Sigma (cc \times f)$ and find the estimated mean.

The table records the masses of $20$ animals.
$\begin{array}{c|c|c}\text{Mass (kg)}&cc&f\\ \hline 40 < m \le 50&45&5\\ 50 < m \le 60&55&10\\ 60 < m \le 70&65&5\end{array}$
Calculate the estimated mean mass.
Why is the mean calculated from a grouped frequency distribution table referred to as an 'estimate' rather than the exact mean?
foundation.solution_text:
Individual data values are lost when data is grouped into intervals.
The calculation assumes every value in a class equals its class centre, which may differ from the true values.

foundation.question_text:
A grouped table for runner ages lists the classes $10-19, 20-29, 30-39,$ and $40+$.
Why is it impossible to calculate an estimate of the mean from this table?
foundation.solution_text: The open-ended class $40+$ has no upper limit, so its class centre cannot be determined.

foundation.question_text:
An ogive shows the cumulative frequencies of test scores for $80$ students.
At what cumulative frequency value should a horizontal line be drawn to estimate the median score?
foundation.solution_text:
$\text{Median position} = 50\% \text{ of } 80$
$= 40$
A horizontal line is drawn from cumulative frequency $40$.

development.question_text:
The commute times (in minutes) of $60$ employees are shown in the table.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Time (min)}&\text{Frequency }(f)\\ \hline 0-9&8\\ 10-19&14\\ 20-29&20\\ 30-39&12\\ 40-49&6\end{array}$
Calculate the estimated mean commute time.

In a survey of $120$ weekly grocery bills, the grouped distribution is:
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Bill (\$)}&\text{Frequency }(f)\\ \hline 50 \le x < 100&18\\ 100 \le x < 150&42\\ 150 \le x < 200&36\\ 200 \le x < 250&24\end{array}$
Identify the modal class and determine the median class.
development.solution_text:
The greatest frequency is $42$, so $\text{Modal class} = \$100 \le x < \$150$.
$\text{Middle positions: } \frac{120}{2} = 60\text{ and }61$
$\text{Cumulative frequencies: }18,60,96,120$
The $60\text{th}$ bill lies in $\$100 \le x < \$150$, and the $61\text{st}$ bill lies in $\$150 \le x < \$200$.
The median is the average of these two bills. Their exact values are unknown, so their average could lie in either class; the table does not determine a unique median class.
The ogive method instead estimates the median by reading across from cumulative frequency $60$, which gives the boundary value $\$150$.

$\text{Median position} = 50\% \text{ of } 100$
$= 50$
Read horizontally from cumulative frequency $50$ to the ogive, then down to the mark axis.
$\text{Estimated median} \approx 47.5\text{ marks}$

development.question_text:
The table gives the weekly wages of $50$ apprentices.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Weekly wage (\$)}&\text{Frequency }(f)\\ \hline 600-699&10\\ 700-799&18\\ 800-899&16\\ 900-999&6\end{array}$
Calculate the estimated mean weekly wage.

The table shows the masses of animals at a shelter.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Mass (kg)}&\text{Frequency }(f)\\ \hline 0 < m \le 10&3\\ 10 < m \le 20&7\\ 20 < m \le 30&8\\ 30 < m \le 40&2\end{array}$
Calculate the estimated mean mass.

development.solution_text:
$\text{Median position} = 50\% \text{ of } 60$
$= 30$
Read horizontally from cumulative frequency $30$ to the ogive, then down to the battery life axis.
$\text{Estimated median} \approx 7.0\text{ hours}$

development.question_text:
A dataset of $5$ observations in the class $10-20$ ($cc = 15$) has actual values $11, 11, 12, 13, 13$.
Calculate the exact mean of these $5$ values, compare it to the class centre, and explain why the grouped estimate is higher.
development.solution_text:
$\text{Exact mean} = \frac{11 + 11 + 12 + 13 + 13}{5}$
$= \frac{60}{5}$
$= 12$
$\text{Grouped estimate} = cc = 15$
The grouped estimate is $3$ units higher because all actual values lie in the lower half of the interval ($11-13$), but the calculation replaces them all with the midpoint $15$.

mastery.question_text:
The table shows the masses of $40$ parcels.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Mass (kg)}&\text{Frequency }(f)\\ \hline 0 < m \le 4&7\\ 4 < m \le 10&11\\ 10 < m \le 20&13\\ 20 < m \le 40&9\end{array}$
Calculate the estimated mean mass.

A repair shop analyses customer invoices (in dollars):
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Cost (\$)}&\text{Frequency }(f)\\ \hline 100-199&12\\ 200-299&25\\ 300-399&38\\ 400-499&15\\ 500-599&10\end{array}$
Find the modal class, the median class, and the estimated mean invoice cost.
mastery.solution_text:
$\text{Modal class} = \$300 - \$399\text{ (highest frequency } 38\text{)}$
$\text{Middle positions: } \frac{100}{2} = 50\text{ and }51$
$\text{Cumulative frequencies: } 12, 37, 75, 90, 100$
The $50\text{th}$ and $51\text{st}$ invoices both lie in the third class, $\$300 - \$399$.
$\text{Median class} = \$300 - \$399$
$\text{Class centres: } 149.5, 249.5, 349.5, 449.5, 549.5$
$\Sigma (cc \times f) = (149.5 \times 12) + (249.5 \times 25) + (349.5 \times 38) + (449.5 \times 15) + (549.5 \times 10)$
$= 1794 + 6237.5 + 13281 + 6742.5 + 5495$
$= 33550$
$\overline{x} = \frac{33550}{100}$
$= \$335.50$

mastery.question_text:
An actual dataset of $50$ test marks has a true mean of $64.2$, but the estimated mean calculated using class centres is $62.8$.
Provide a mathematically sound explanation for why the estimated mean is lower than the true mean.
mastery.solution_text:
The estimated mean replaces every score in a class with that class's midpoint ($cc$).
If the actual scores inside several classes are skewed towards the upper limits of their intervals, the true values exceed the midpoints, making the true mean higher than the estimated mean.
